questions.question_text: According to the Children’s Bureau of the Department of Health and Human Services, which is the most common form of abuse suffered by children?

options.text: Emotional
Physical
Neglect
Sexual
Ritual

questions.explanation: According to the Children’s Bureau of the Department of Health and Human Services, of the 3.6 million child abuse cases reported each year, 78 percent are cases of neglect[cite: 15]. The results are published in an annual document called Child Maltreatment[cite: 15]. The agency estimated that approximately 3.6 million alleged victims were reported to child protective services[cite: 15]. Of those reports, approximately 22.1 percent were substantiated[cite: 15]. The substantiated cases were distributed as follows: 78 percent neglect, 18 percent physical abuse, 9.5 percent sexual abuse, and 7.6 percent emotional or psychological maltreatment[cite: 15]. The Children’s Bureau estimated that 1,770 children died as the result of maltreatment in 2009[cite: 15]. Approximately 46 percent of these deaths were children younger than 1 year of age[cite: 15]. Approximately 12 percent of the fatalities had been identified as victims and received family preservation services in the prior 5 years, and 2 percent had been removed from foster care and reunited with their families in the prior 5 years[cite: 15].

questions.question_text:
Rights to legal counsel, Fifth Amendment privilege, and notice of charges
A. Juvenile court system
B. Adult court system

options.text: if the item is associated with A only
if the item is associated with B only
if the item is associated with both A and B
if the item is associated with neither A nor B

correct_answer.text: if the item is associated with both A and B

correct_answers.text: if the item is associated with both A and B

questions.explanation: Both the juvenile court and the adult court systems must conform to the same rights of due process, which include the right to notice of charges, right to legal counsel, the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination, and the right to confront witnesses[cite: 15]. The adult court system uses the following process: pretrial hearing, trial, and sentencing[cite: 15]. The juvenile court system differs and includes intake, adjudication, and disposition[cite: 15]. If a juvenile makes a confession, disposition may proceed without the trial[cite: 15]. The adult court system uses both trial by jury and trial by judge without a jury in its decision making, but in juvenile court, all trials are decided by a judge without a jury[cite: 15].

questions.question_text: Young children are usually better off with their mothers.

options.text: “Tender-years” doctrine
“Best interests of the child” doctrine

questions.explanation: Child custody disputes throughout recorded history have reflected a society’s view of children in families[cite: 15]. The practice of courts becoming involved in private family affairs is fairly recent[cite: 15]. The history of these issues traces a change from seeing children as essentially owned by their parents to considering what is likely to be in the child’s best interests[cite: 15]. Judicial decisions have been informed by various doctrines, including the “tender-years” and the “best interests of the child” doctrines[cite: 15]. The “tender-years” doctrine existed well into the 20th century and held that young children (from birth to about age 7 years) were usually better off with their mothers, who were presumed to be best able to raise and nurture their offspring[cite: 15]. With this doctrine in mind, most custody decisions were made in the mother’s favor[cite: 15]. This presumption was replaced in the last third of the 20th century by the “best interests of the child” doctrine, which is the current law in the United States[cite: 15]. This doctrine holds that the focus of a child custody case should be the child and that courts should not lean toward one parent or the other based exclusively on gender[cite: 15]. Considerations of the optimal parent for the child expanded beyond mother-child relationship and included assessing issues of emotional climate, safety, and educational and social opportunities for the children[cite: 15]. There may be situations in which “best interest of the child” dictates that custody should reside with a nonparent rather than a parent[cite: 15].

questions.question_text: Specified that the standard “beyond a reasonable doubt” must be followed in delinquency hearings

options.text: “In re Gault” case
“In re Winship” case
Tarasoff I and Tarasoff II rulings
Education for All Handicapped Children Act of 1975

questions.explanation:
Knowledge of the juvenile court system and its strengths and weaknesses is essential for forensic child and adolescent psychiatrists[cite: 15]. Clinicians must also appreciate the indications for waiver hearings and the grounds for judicial determination that a minor be tried as an adult[cite: 15]. Although the juvenile court system operated for decades as supposedly child oriented and protective, the U.S. Supreme Court, in the landmark case “In re Gault,” determined that the system sometimes does not accord juveniles rights equal to those of adults[cite: 15]. This decision held that in delinquency cases, juveniles must be accorded basic due process rights, including the right to notice of charges, the right to legal counsel, the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination, and the right to confront witnesses[cite: 15]. Another important Supreme Court case, “In re Winship,” held that that standard “beyond a reasonable doubt” must be followed in delinquency hearings[cite: 15].
Child and adolescent psychiatrists may be involved in forensic evaluations outside the more common venues of the family or criminal court[cite: 15]. For example, they may be called upon to make certain recommendations for a student with disabilities under the landmark Education for All Handicapped Children Act of 1975[cite: 15]. This law requires that all children with disabilities, regardless of the severity of their condition, be provided a free and appropriate public education in the least restrictive environment[cite: 15]. Children with disabilities are defined as those who are mentally retarded, learning disabled, physically disabled, or emotionally disturbed[cite: 15]. A treating or evaluating child psychiatrist may be asked to testify at various hearings required under the law[cite: 15]. Knowledge of the law’s implications as well as of the particular child will be critical to performing a proper evaluation[cite: 15].
Most clinicians working with children and adolescents spell out the limits of confidentiality to the families they work with at the outset of treatment and clarify how communications with parents are to be handled; they may particularly need to review limits of confidentiality with respect to insurance plans[cite: 15]. Additional limits to confidentiality include behavior harmful to self or others[cite: 15]. When disclosures need to be made to parents, the patient may be given the option of telling them him- or herself or of having the discussion together with the parents and the patient[cite: 15]. Other exceptions to confidentiality include a law on reporting child abuse, which is mandatory in all states[cite: 15]. A physician who fails to report suspicion of abuse may be liable for civil as well as criminal sanction[cite: 15]. If an abuse report needs to be filed, parents should be informed[cite: 15]. In some states, physicians have a duty to protect third parties, as specified under Tarasoff I and Tarasoff II, the 1976 and 1982 rulings of the California Supreme Court in the two cases of Tarasoff v. Regents of University of California[cite: 15].
